utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before we proceed today, the order which we made in relation to FWS-137 who was to be heard by videolink included an order that for technical reasons he had to be heard in a closed Court. We have rescinded the order that he be heard by way of videolink, and we must now also rescind the order that he be heard in a closed court. He will have facial distortion and all the usual things, but it will be in open court. Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you're examining the witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't hear the Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you say something at this time, sir? Did you respond to that answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At least in his language I heard something, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, we've got a technical problem, then.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right. It's all right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Very well, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before the break you had told us already that about 40 to 50 days after your arrival in the KP Dom, a first so-called exchange took place, and you mentioned that you saw Pero Elez in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher -- oh, he's gone. With the help of my assistant, I will put a photo to you, and it's the Exhibit 18, photo 7477.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you point out --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It seems that the monitor is not working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This courtroom is sent to try us, rather than the accused, I'm afraid. Just turn it on, would you? See if there's a button that turns it on. THE USHER: It's not from here, it should be from the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If somebody in the booth could turn on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's coming through on what is being broadcast but it is not coming through on the ELMO. The ELMO has a sign which rather misleadingly says that we are in closed session, or it may be we're in recess, but it's certainly wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can proceed without the photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it might be advisable.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It may be all day before we get some help here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, where did you see Pero Elez in the compound?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the metal door which led to the entrance of the KP Dom. That's, that's the area where I saw him before -- after that entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him in front of the metal door in the yard, or did you see him standing in the door where?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before that door, inside the courtyard of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he accompanied by prison staff; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was accompanied by some of his own soldiers and maybe there was a guard in his entourage

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know Pero Elez from before the war, or did you get to know him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him well. He comes from Budanj. He lived in Foca. He used to work in the KP Dom before the war, and he was retired as a member of the staff of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he take the detainees with him through this metal door?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot remember exactly how many people were called out. I can remember three persons, Kemal Niksic, Salko Sljivo, and Dzamal Niksic. They were in that group, but there were other men as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was said why the detainees were taken? Did you get any explanation why they had to follow Pero Elez?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later, stories did the rounds alleging that Pero Elez was supposed to take a group of people to the mine to enable the mine to start operating again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who said that? Detainees or guards or both?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those prisoners could not tell those stories because they had no contact with me, but sometimes stories like that would leak from the guards themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the mine operational at that time; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was operational, but I know that it was only after a while that a group from the KP Dom was sent to work in the mine. I don't think the mine was operational at the start. They were trying to activate the open pit of that mine in the beginning, and that was approximately at the end of 1992, in the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you went to Miljevina to work and prepare machinery in the mine, did you see any of these men, these detainees who had been taken on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw a single person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did any of them return to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned these particular three persons. Did you ever hear of them again from their relatives or from whatever source?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no trace of these persons. They were never heard of again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever observe detainees being taken for an exchange while you were working in the metalwork shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were exchanges, but when we would come back, for instance, for this -- from this forced labour, and some people who never left their rooms would tell us a group had been taken out there and there. But we didn't actually know it was for an exchange, and we looked from our windows at a vehicle parked just outside the KP Dom. It was a military vehicle like a truck, a covered truck, and after a while this vehicle would set off towards the town. Sevko Kubat and I would watch this from our metal shop. And after the vehicle set off, we noticed a vehicle which had been parked all the time on the other bank of the Drina. That vehicle was full of soldiers, and that vehicle would also be started and follow the other vehicle. And after the working hours when we left the workshop, the -- our colleagues would tell us that it was an exchange which had taken place. Of course, we didn't know the details. We didn't know where -- which people had been taken out and where, but there was no trace of these people again. Nobody ever heard of them again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did this happen that you saw the trucks? Do you recall the month, maybe?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really remember well because it was a long time ago, but it may have been in 1993, March, April perhaps. I cannot tell you the exact date or month, but it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you could see, you and your colleague Sevko Kubat, could see. How could you see? How could you look over the wall of the -- that surrounded the metal shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This mechanical section of the metalwork shop, metalwork shop was slightly elevated relative to the metalwork shop itself, and we could see well the entrance to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Unfortunately we cannot use the ELMO now, but the part of the metalwork shop where you worked, is it more to the -- is it further away from the gate or is it the closest part of the metalwork shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the end of the metalwork shop, nearer to the gate. The mechanical shop is the last section of the metalwork shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The mechanical shop, is that where you were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that you saw trucks. The first truck, where was it when you saw it and noticed it for the first time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right at the entrance to the KP Dom, a covered truck. It was right next to the wall.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see detainees board this truck? Could you see that from your position?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we couldn't see because it was a covered vehicle. It had a roof.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did other detainees work in the metalwork shop closer to the gate so that they could see better than you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they could see, but in any case, they were much closer than we were in the mechanical shop.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were ever members of the metalwork shop taken away for exchange?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was one time, one afternoon when we had returned from the metalwork shop. We went straight to lunch, and after lunch we were locked up in that working room. And after a while, a guard came, I don't remember which one, but I think it was Zoran Vukovic, and he called out a number of persons who were in the metalwork shop in that afternoon, and an exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when? Can you say when this happened? Was it in 1992 or 1993? Could you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was 1992. I'm not sure which month. It could have been August or September, approximately. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How many members of the work group were taken away on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many persons. I can mention Suad Islambasic, Karasi, Uzeir Hadzialic. I can't remember any other men at this moment, but there were more of them. Smajo Dzevdas and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see who took them away? Were they soldiers, or could you simply see the guards taking them out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who came and called out their names was, I think, Zoran Vukovic. There were two Zoran Vukovics inside the compound, actually, but I mean Zoran Vukovic from Josanica, the dark-haired guard. He came and called out those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did Mr. Goljanin react to this fact that some of his workers were taken away for an exchange?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning when we were about to taken to the metalwork shop, somebody from the compound would normally come to take people to work, to cut grass, to the forest, or to the farm or wherever. One guard would take one group. That morning Relja Goljanin came to pick us up, and he was surprised to see how few of us were left, and he asked, "Where are the others?" And we told him the story. We told him about the exchange which took place the previous afternoon, and we explained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he react in any way? Did he say something or did he do something after that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment he didn't say anything. He only took us to the metalwork shop, but Relja Goljanin reappeared after a while with Savo Todovic, and as I said, we were at the end of the metalwork shop. They were going from one section to another with a piece of paper; we didn't know what it was until he reached us. When he came up to us, he asked us about our names, dates of birth, and other details, and they took them down. So they took our personal details at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said "they took the details down." On what? In a book or on a piece of paper, or what was it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wrote these things on a piece of paper and they took it away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was any other worker of the work group taken away after this one incident?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I'm not sure. I don't know if that group included Ramiz Maljanovic and the person, if I can use a piece of paper, there are other people. I think Ramiz Maljanovic was taken away, and Rasim Taranin as well, but I'm not sure whether they had been in the metalwork shop at that time. And the people who remained, remained there until our exchange in the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Q. Sir, you have this sheet of paper in front of you that we had actually started with. There is this group of people with the same last name, and you told us these were some relatives of you, and I do not want you to mention the names. What happened -- what became of these people? Did they survive the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of those people, no one survived the KP Dom, and they had been taken away for various exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we've been informed by the video booth that the ELMO is now working, for which we're very grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, but we have concluded this description of the exchange, and I think he has made clear where he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you testified in the previous case, you mentioned that you were arrested together with another father and a son. When you described your arrest, you said on a previous occasion, in another trial, that you were arrested, you and 77 -- [redacted] were arrested, and [redacted] father and son. What happened to this [redacted] father and son? Did they survive the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. And before, before that, another of his sons had been brought in which means that this father and his two sons did not survive the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What happened to them? Were they also taken away in a so-called exchange, or what?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all taken for an exchange. We were actually looking forward to those exchanges, thinking that one day our turn would come. However, there were very few actual exchanges, real exchanges. In most cases, they were fatal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, in your previous testimony you have already described the beatings in the KP Dom, and I do not want to repeat all this evidence here. The question that I have is, did any persons return to your room with obvious signs of beatings? Do you recall anybody?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the setting up of the work platoon, I was in Room 16. Two people were taken away from that room. One Mandzo, I don't know his first name, but he was a nurse, I believe; and a man from Josanica whose name I don't really know. He was called Kalabic. They were taken for an interrogation, and when they came back, they had obvious signs of beatings. And this young man, Mandzo in particular, who was a nurse, he carried his shoes in his hands, and he barely made it across the yard. One of his fingers, I don't know on which hand, was broken. And this other man, Kalabic, was badly beaten in his chest and his back, and there was something like a crack on his neck. And they were in the same room as Dr. Amir Berberkic who tried to give them some basic assistance, and he stitched up the laceration on Kalabic's neck. And they used thread to fix the broken finger of the other man. Kalabic had returned from a solitary confinement cell badly beaten up, and at the end of his tether. Also in my room there was Zaim Cedic who was badly beaten up. He was there when I got there. And those are the people I remember from that room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At what time were this Mandzo and this Kalabic, at what time were they taken out, during the evening or during the daytime, for this Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. interrogation that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was in the middle of the day, and we could see them both being taken out and being brought back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In between this period when you saw them being taken and when they were returned, did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as those God damn metal doors would close, in most cases we would hear screams, cries for help. Not always, but most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to this Mandzo and Kalabic, did you hear these cries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't see them screaming because they must have been taken to the administrative building where they were interrogated. We could only see them coming back. We could see the state they were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My question was actually, did you hear them scream, not that you saw them, what happened to them. Did you hear them scream?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I said that already. I couldn't hear any sounds related to the two of them, but I could only see them coming back, and I told you I saw this Mandzo in a very bad state carrying his shoes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the person Mandzo, the nurse, the Prosecution believes that is number B-37; and Kalabic, that is a person who other witnesses have mentioned, the real name is Hasan Dzano, and it's B-18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the person Zaim Cedic mentioned by the Witness is B-11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzano, Dzano, right. You put it nicely.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you said you were detained until the 4th of October, 1994. What happened on this day? How were you taken away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the 5th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, the 5th. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Miljevina at that moment. I remember this well. It was raining on that morning. I was supposed to work in Kute on a Ford vehicle. They had got spare parts for the engine that I was supposed to put together. Since the spare parts were not right, of course I could not work on that day. Stevanovic nicknamed Sumar was with me. He was the one who got these parts, and since they were no good, he returned them to Miljevina. As we arrived at the motel in Miljevina, I don't know who walked up to us. They said they're looking for [redacted] at the KP Dom, and they said that it was in connection with some kind of exchange. And then they said "You wait here," they went to a different room, and then there was a telephone call which I did not manage to hear. I heard that there was a telephone conversation going on, but I couldn't hear what was being said. After that, he returned and said, "They're looking for you at the KP Dom, and you have to get all your things." He went to see me off to the police station. After I got out of the police station, after I got into his vehicle, he said, "All of you are going to be exchanged." Then we travelled to Foca. Halfway, after Kute, a vehicle from the KP Dom caught up with us with the new warden, Zoran Sekulovic in it, and yet another person; I can't remember who that was. There were two people there. "They wanted to leave you behind, so that's why I came to pick you up." And that's how we all returned together to the KP Dom. When I got back, everybody was dressed, everybody was ready. They told me that my son was waiting for me in the room, and they told me to get ready, and that's the way it was. When I got back, we all got onto the bus, and of course, we set out for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: After having reached Sarajevo, were you returned to Miljevina again, all the detainees on the bus?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we reached Sarajevo, Kula, when we were supposed to get out and report with the Red Cross -- actually, in the meantime as we travelled and passed Rogoj, by Rogoj we were overtaken by a police car that honked its horn, and I realised that it was the commander from Miljevina because I knew the vehicle and everything. They didn't stop us there. The vehicle disappeared right in front of us. And then this person, Pedo, reappeared at Kula itself with another man. I think it's Fundup. Also this person had weapons. It was no longer a police Golf, it was a Lada Niva this time. Then they gave us orders that we all had to go back, and they said things like, "Whoever had to get money for an exchange and whatever," so then really we were taken back to Miljevina. Then he said on the way, "Serb young people are getting killed, and money is being taken for these exchanges. All of these people should be taken to Rogoj and executed." That's the gist of what he said, you see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "he," you mean this Pedo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How was this situation then solved in Miljevina? Who solved it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody went silent after that threat of his. We were all worried, and we all wondered how things would end after what he said. As we reached Rogoj, he was standing there on his own. The driver stopped again. He threatened us. He said don't look here, otherwise I'm going to tear off your heads with bursts of gunfire." So that's how this conversation ended. The driver ignited the engine, and then we went to Miljevina. The vehicle was parked there, and we were joined by a soldier from Rogoj, I think. And he escorted our bus to Miljevina. He was by the bus --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just a moment. We would not need all the details, the question was --

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Details?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How was the situation solved? Who actually solved the situation in Miljevina so that you could return and be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably after that, delegations came. I don't know who was on this delegation from Foca itself, and a meeting was held at the motel. So it was decided once again that we would be returned for an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On this occasion in Miljevina, did you see staff from the KP Dom? Did they also -- were they also one of the delegations that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. On the first escort there were some people from the KP Dom. I can't remember exactly. And also on the bus itself, there were two persons from the city police, from the town police, two persons. And also the vehicle from the KP Dom, I don't know who escorted this vehicle, but as for down there, I don't know about all these authorities. Probably military authorities from the KP Dom. I don't know who made up this delegation. I mean, the delegation that engaged in these negotiations and that passed a decision to have an exchange take place again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Sekulovic on this occasion in Miljevina when there were these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's now talk about some persons from the staff of the KP Dom. Who was the warden before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Radojica Tesovic. I think, but I'm not sure, but I think it was Radojica Tesovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Tesovic in the KP Dom during your confinement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of our exchange, once or twice I may have seen Mr. Tesovic at the farm; however, throughout that period at the KP Dom, I hardly ever saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already described that you saw Mr. Krnojelac driving in the warden's car. Did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, very often. Not far away from my apartment where I lived was the elementary school where Mr. Krnojelac was a teacher at Gornji Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you know where he lived before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact address.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you hear that his house was destroyed or did you even see that his house was destroyed during the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that, and rumour had it that it was practically at the very outset, perhaps even among the first houses. I did not see this, but I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did he live during the war, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war? People talked, or rather, after I was exchanged my wife told me that he lived in Dr. Ismet Sosevic's apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Dr. Ismet Sosevic, is that a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said your wife told you that he lived in Dr. Sosevic's apartment. When did she tell you that and how did she know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she told me about that only after my exchange, or rather, our exchange. And she knew through her neighbours because, after all, she did stay there for a long time. I think she stayed in Foca until September 1992. September, October, I'm not sure. I'm not sure about the exact date when she got out.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you learn about the fact that Mr. Krnojelac was living in this doctor's apartment? Did she approach him there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you -- do you have some information that this is going to get us somewhere? Is it seems to me to be complete hearsay upon hearsay and probably upon hearsay. If there's something in the statement which suggests that there's going to be some probative value in this, you proceed; but it seems to me we're just flogging a very dead horse on this particular point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness will testify that his wife tried to approach Mr. Krnojelac there to get her son released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's see what you can get from the witness about that, but otherwise, it's of no probative value.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did your wife try to approach Mr. Krnojelac to get -- and if so, why?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in a way, she tried through her neighbours, her ethnic Serb neighbours. At least, to set her son free. However, after the tragedy that befell his sons and some other persons, these persons themselves said that the time would not be right for that kind of a visit and that kind of a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden. When did you learn that and how?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, practically everybody -- practically all the guards addressed Warden Krnojelac as warden, so on the basis of that information and also by virtue of the fact that the car was brought for a repair, it was said that the warden's car had to be checked, oil, water, batteries, the tyres should be pumped up, et cetera. So through these orders we realised that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden. Also, when Mr. Zoran Sekulovic came, he said that he had replaced the warden, that he was the new warden now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually speak with Mr. Krnojelac while you were detained and while he was the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. As a matter of fact, I think that hardly any one of the detainees talked to the warden. It was always indirect communication, through someone, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac in the metalwork shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come, but he never addressed us directly. He would come to Relja Goljanin's office and then he'd leave the metalwork shop again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see him talk with Mr. Goljanin or the guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did they behave towards Mr. Krnojelac? Was it a respectful manner, was it -- in which way, when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to explain that. These were conversations that boiled down to issuing orders, things like that. I can't really give you the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said that it boiled down to issuing orders. Who was issuing orders to whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that he really cannot say what they talked about, and now he's being asked to concretely say who issued orders to who, but this was only his assumption. That's what the witness said, that he only assumed that. And the witness said that he did not know whether he was issuing -- whether orders were being issued or whether they were reaching agreement on something that he did not know about that. That would be a more accurate version of the transcript. I didn't want to react at first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the transcript is wrong, because the transcript itself does not suggest that. It says, "These were conversations that boiled down to issuing orders, things like that. I can't really give you the gist of it." In other words, the terms of it. I don't see that the question is improperly based. When it says, "You said that it boiled down to issuing orders." That's exactly what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I did not want to interrupt, but the transcript did not include everything he said. Whether they were issuing orders or whether they were reaching agreement, that I don't know. That is the first thing the witness said. And also, he was not sure whether they were issuing orders or whether they were discussing something like -- something different. And then the question was a leading question, "Who was issuing orders to who?" The witness did not say that specifically. My learned colleague then asked who was issuing orders to who, and the witness did not say with any certainty that orders were being issued to someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bakrac, I think you and I will probably go to our graves disagreeing about what a leading question is. If the witness says, "That boiled down to issuing orders," then the Prosecution is entitled to ask who issued the orders. That's not a leading question. You proceed, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you heard my last question: Who issued orders to whom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I can answer. I only know about my work. I could never issue orders to my foreman or my boss. It is always my foreman or my boss that issued orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: So you got orders from your foreman. Do you know who gave orders to your foreman?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Probably somebody that he was subordinated to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I know we allow a certain amount of hearsay, but this is getting into very dangerous ground to be asking questions like that. How would he know? If I may suggest to you, and this is perhaps an old common lawyer putting it this way, we should first of all determine whether he can give us some direct evidence. He heard somebody giving the order, to give these further orders on. Then it would come in as direct evidence, or, at least, firsthand hearsay. But you are inviting him to speculate, really, and the answer which he gave clearly indicates that he is speculating. Now, I realise this is an important part, but it's important also to get it in properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me formulate it this way: When you received your order from Goljanin or the foreman that you mentioned, did they ever tell you who ordered them to give you that particular task? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a few cases -- this is the third time I'm telling you about the vehicle. As for the other jobs, it was Goljanin who directly issued orders, the person who was in charge of the metalwork shop. How can I tell? In exceptional cases, these were very rare cases, that he would say, "The warden said that you should prepare his car, that the oil should be changed, that the car should be prepared for a journey," things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw Mr. Krnojelac, what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac regularly wore an olive-green/gray uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mean a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never did, as far as bigger weapons are concerned. He only had a pistol or something like that. At least, I never saw him with, say, a rifle or an automatic rifle or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see the pistol on him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At what times did you see him? Did you ever see him in the evening or late afternoon?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before I was taken to this metal group or metalwork shop, that was perhaps 40 days, they regularly came to eat within the compound because the dining room was for detainees, and there was a dining room for the guards. But in between these two dining rooms, there was the kitchen. So everybody came there for meals and that's when I would see Warden Krnojelac most often within the compound. I could see him outside on a few occasions as well as I was going to the metalwork shop and coming back.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was with him when you saw Mr. Krnojelac in the yard or outside of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a bit difficult. Well, with guards, of course, but then it's hard to tell going from one person to another when which person was with the warden because it's been quite a bit of time now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see the warden with Mr. Rasevic and Mr. Todovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be in their company.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac in the company of military personnel?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once, I think. Again, I am going back to the time before I was taken away. About a platoon of soldiers came in uniform with weapons, and then we were terrified, too, we were wondering what would happen. They had placed some mines on some of the green areas within the walls, and I think that then he was in the compound, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean he was -- he happened to be in the compound by chance, or did he actually accompany these soldiers? When did you see him with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't define that, whether that was by accident or whether he actually entered because that group came. That is hard for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw these soldiers in the compound, was Mr. Krnojelac with them for quite some time, or did they just pass? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly how much time he spent there with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Krnojelac with politicians, in the company of politicians?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It happened, though, on one occasion, although I don't remember who it was exactly, we were in the mess room having lunch. A person came wearing civilian clothes with a moustache. It was a short man. He said, "Enjoy your meal," and he introduced himself as the Minister of Justice. I don't remember who was accompanying this person.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you continue to see Mr. Krnojelac after he was replaced by Mr. Sekulovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely. By chance. But I never saw him again within the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you see him? Did you see him near the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is a restaurant right across which is part of the KP Dom, and that's where I saw him once or twice after his replacement, at the time when we were going to have this snack or coming back from it. That is when I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was he wearing when you saw him on these two, one or two occasions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was wearing civilian clothes then. I'm not sure. I think he was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he go into the restaurant, or what did you see him do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a very short time coming from the -- getting out of the KP Dom and getting inside. I had no time to stop and watch what he was doing. It's very difficult to answer this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did any of the guards or the KP Dom staff tell you what Mr. Krnojelac's new job was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not one, but several of them claimed that Mr. Krnojelac was occupying a new position.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't really understand what the witness said after the words "new position." What he said seems improbable.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please repeat your answer. What did the guards tell you what Mr. Krnojelac's new position was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- they said he was working in the wrong police. I don't know exactly what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do you mean by "wrong police"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I meant the border police, not the wrong police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who told you that? Which guard, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, it's difficult to say after nine years, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the border police actually frequent the restaurant that you just mentioned, the restaurant of the KP Dom? Did they actually go there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allegedly they did. That is something I found out about from a person who went there to clean. His name was Dudic. He told me they were spending nights in that building of the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This person Dudic, is he -- what is it, Dudic? This person, was he a detainee?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Savo Todovic, what was his exact function in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Savo Todovic's job was to coordinate with the working group, and we had the impression that he was the one selecting men for the working group.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me cite from a statement that you gave to the Prosecutor's Office dated the 17th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And for the interpreter, it's page 10, paragraph 3 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this statement, it is taken down as your words, "Although Krnojelac was the director, it seemed that Todovic Savo was actually in charge. I say this because he was directing who was going where and who was doing what." Can you explain this sentence? Is it how it was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I have already answered this partly in my previous answer. In everything concerning work and work relations, Savo Todovic was in charge. He decided who was going to work and whether he was going to work at all. And at least, that was our opinion, because Krnojelac never interfered with those things. He would never come and speak directly to prisoners, whereas Savo Todovic did that. And there was an undertone of threat in his voice when he spoke to us. For instance, he would say, "How long do you intend to keep lying about? It's time to go to work." And as far as work is concerned, I think Savo Todovic was more important for us than Krnojelac, even, because he would issue direct orders. He would very often have direct contact with prisoners, and this sentence from my statement was in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are the questions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will take the reverse order, taking up the things that are freshest in the mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to introduce myself to the witness. I am Mihajlo Bakrac, one of the Defence counsel of the accused Krnojelac and since we have already had problems before with the interpreters and until now you have waited to hear the interpretation of the questions asked by my learned friend, we will now potentially encounter even greater problems because you will have to wait for the interpretation so that everybody understands us. I will take the reverse order, as I said, and we'll come back to the last question asked by my colleague. My learned friend just mentioned to you the last statement you gave in November, on the 17th of November, 1995, something you said about the warden, Mr. Krnojelac, and Savo Todovic, and she asked you to explain what you meant when you said that it seemed to you that it was actually Savo Todovic who was in charge. But it seems that my learned friend did not present to you another statement that you gave on the 3rd of December, 1998, in which you spoke exclusively and very thoroughly about the structure of administration of the KP Dom as you saw it. I will read out to you a statement from that second statement, and you will tell me whether you really stated that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is page 3 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It seemed to me that Savo Todovic had a higher position than Krnojelac, and he was in charge of the work obligations of prisoners." Did you really state that it seemed to you that Savo Todovic held a higher position than Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer this specifically now. When I said that, I meant direct dealings with the work platoon were handled by Savo Todovic, is what I meant. Mr. Krnojelac didn't interfere with that. And who is subordinate to whom is difficult to say. A warden can be -- can hold a higher position than a clerk. It cannot be vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What I'm interested in is, is it true that you stated what I just read out to you, that it seemed to you that Todovic had held a higher position than Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but precisely in the context which I just explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please, please. You are both coming in too early, both of you. Now, if I can speak to the witness first, do you have the transcript coming up in front of you on the screen there? Do you have typing there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you would wait until the question has finished being typed out, then that is when you should answer it. Mr. Bakrac, you know that you must wait, too. Please.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, did you know what the exact administration structure in the KP Dom was? Did anybody present any papers to you about that, or did anyone report to you what that structure was, or is this entirely your observation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever presented to me an official report about the structure of the KP Dom, but according to the conversations and stories told by the guards who handled prisoners within the KP Dom and handled the working group, we knew what the relations were among people, who was commander of the guard, who was the warden. We knew all this, although nobody ever officially explained it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, you just said that this impression that Savo Todovic held a higher position than Krnojelac, you explained where this impression came from. Was it also based on the fact that without consulting anyone, Savo Todovic meted out punishment in the compound for workers in the metalwork shop? He said, "You'll get 15 days, you'll get 20." Isn't that so? Wasn't his behaviour in such situations reason for you to get that impression?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically, I always speak about the working platoon because that's what I know best. Savo Todovic was the one who designated who will go to work where. And even when he meted out punishment, he did so of his own accord without seeking anyone's approval because he was in charge of workers and work relations. And he decided on those punishments arbitrarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said the working group. Did Savo Todovic hold a speech to all prisoners of the KP Dom, or only to the working group in the incident described earlier?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when -- because Ekrem Zekovic had escaped from the metalwork shop, the people working the metalwork shop were taken out for interrogation, which means that he was threatening people from the metalwork shop. Not the entire work platoon because the work platoon also included people who went to work in the mine, people who went out to cut grass, people who went out to the forest, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, remember that we have a voice distortion here. If you leave your microphone on, it cancels out the voice distortion. I know it's going to be a nuisance, but it's the only way it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try while fighting time, interpreters, and so on, to take care of time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, does that mean that within the compound of the KP Dom in the courtyard when Ekrem Zekovic was caught, that Savo Todovic held his speech and presented Ekrem Zekovic only to people from the metalwork shop, or all the prisoners who were in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about other rooms. I said in my previous statement already that while we were in solitary cells, they went from room to room and displayed Ekrem Zekovic. I don't know what these people were told. I can only say what we from the metalwork shop were told when we were taken out, what we were told about Ekrem Zekovic, and what he said to us later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please tell me, who was involved in the interrogation of people on the occasion of the escape of Ekrem Zekovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the escape of Ekrem Zekovic, we were taken out. I described this in part already. The guards exchanged remarks and threatened us. That started in the cell where I was and continued in the hallway and in the solitary cells. People were taken out from solitary cells and interrogated one by one. Who was involved in the interrogation of individuals, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You just said, sir, that you heard from the guards who was who. I will take you back to your statement of the 3rd December, 1998, where in paragraph 4 at the beginning you say, "I know that Krnojelac was warden of the KP Dom because that was common knowledge. Everybody knew that, although Serbs did not exactly advertise that fact." What is correct, were you not informed or did Serbs not advertise this fact?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would it refresh your memory if I presented it to you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you read it out again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please, please. Just pause, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I will read it out to you again. "I know that Krnojelac was warden of the KP Dom because that was common knowledge. Everybody knew that, although Serbs did not actually advertise that fact."

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what meaning and whether I gave that statement. A long time has passed. But if I did give that statement, I may have meant that apart from the administration and people who went out to work, other people could not have such information. And at the outset, I believe there were rooms where people did not go out at all for months on end, for a month or two months, even. We who worked could get some information precisely from the guards. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, did Krnojelac ever come to the room where you were detained, and did you ever see him in prisoners' quarters?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sure that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Please wait a little for the interpretation. Sir, when representatives of the Red Cross came, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was with them? Who accompanied the representatives of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I remember there was Rasevic, there was Sekulovic. There were more of them when the Red Cross just came.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say Sekulovic. Which Sekulovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember his name, but it was one of the guards. And I believe the last one to leave the room left through the intervention of the Red Cross, and he was the last to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who was the last to leave?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Sekulovic, Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who ordered the guards to put you in a solitary confinement cell when Ekrem Zekovic escaped?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Ekrem Zekovic escaped, nearly everyone gathered: the guards, the commander of the guards, deputies of the commander, Savo Todovic. I cannot really say who issued the order to put people in isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, I will read out to you your statement dated 3rd December, 1998, page 4 of the B/C/S version, paragraph 2, sentence number 3: "We who worked in the metalwork shop, the 14 or 15 of us, were taken there first. Savo Todovic ordered us to be placed in that room."

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was present, but who issued the order, I don't know. And in the hallway just outside the solitary confinement cell there was he and there was Keli, the man nickname Keli. I don't know his last name. We were lined up at the time, and Keli said to Spirjan, Sefik, "We used to be schoolmates and we are nothing any more," and then he punched him in the stomach. And we were later put into solitary cells. Who issued the order, I don't know, because there were two men present, Savo Todovic and Keli.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In your statement which I just quoted, it says, "Savo Todovic ordered us to be placed in that room."

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was there, so it was probably him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you see Savo Todovic address the guards and issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If you saw him addressing the guards and issuing orders, you tell us in which period. I'm asking you, in the time when you were detained down there, did you see Savo Todovic address the guards and issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He specifically issued orders relating to work. Who made the schedules, the rosters for people to go out with working groups, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Savo Todovic invite you for an interview regarding the conduct of some people in the work department?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He invited me one evening. A guard, I don't know which guard, came and told me to go down to the reception area. There were several persons there, and one of them was Savo Todovic. Of course, I said "Good evening, and how are you," and he asked me a question. "How do you deserve your cigarettes and your canned food? What did you do to get them?" And I said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he said then, "Don't hold yourself above others. Don't think that you have any privileges." How could I possibly think I had any privileges when I was in the camp like everyone else? And that was my conversation with Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just before you go on, the interpreters did not get part of that answer. The question which had been asked -- which the witness had asked, "How do you deserve your cigarettes and your canned food? What did you do to get them," we need to know what the answer to that question was that was given by Mr. Todovic. Could you repeat that for us, please, sir? Not the whole of your answer, but what did Todovic say to you when you asked him "How do you deserve your cigarettes and your canned food? What did you do to get them?"

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that, "With people who bring their cars to be repaired, I specifically ask for tinned food and cigarettes in order to do the work at all." He said, "I'm making my work conditional on getting those things." And that's something I never did. It would have never occurred to me to refuse to comply with an order, let alone set my own conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now 11.00, I notice. We'll adjourn now until half past 11. I'm grateful to see that the clock here is now to be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, just before the break you told us about a situation when Mr. Todovic called you. You said that there were some other people there. Can you remember how many and what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the number of persons involved exactly, and I cannot remember these person's names. However, these were people in uniforms, in KP Dom uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were they guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: However, you cannot remember which guards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. Let me explain this to you a bit. When somebody calls you in the evening, you get a bit scared, don't you? You're at your wit's end, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say in the evening. What time was it approximately?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was immediately after dinner. I don't know. It was dark. It was well into the evening. I don't know exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, you talked about the situation when Ekrem Zekovic escaped and when Mr. Ivanovic came and said, "Why didn't you escape, too?" And that you understood this to be a reprimand to the guards that everybody else could have escaped because there were no guards around. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who was accompanying Boro Ivanovic but they passed by us because we were lined up at the very bottom of the metalwork shop. They went towards the mechanical workshop. They went behind it. What they said, I don't know; and what their assessment was, I don't know. But when they passed by us, Boro Ivanovic said precisely those words that I mentioned in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In relation to this, did you also mention in your statement that it seemed to you that Ivanovic outranked the guards and Rasovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know Boro Ivanovic's post exactly. People talked, and some of these stories reached us, too. He was some kind of a security man, at least, that's the information that reached us. How correct this information is, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in your statement you said that it seemed to you that Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac's microphone was off. The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they informed Boro Ivanovic that there had been an escape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, your microphone was off and the interpreters did not hear your question. Can you restate it for their convenience, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour, and I do apologise to you. My hand was faster, and I turned off the microphone before I finished putting my question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you, sir, whether it is correct when you spoke in your statement about what Mr. Ivanovic was saying, that it seemed to you that Ivanovic outranked the guards and Rasevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since Boro Ivanovic had been informed about Ekrem Zekovic's escape, that was our conclusion. We thought that he was above these other persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In terms of the statement that I've just quoted to you, you said that you sometimes heard from the administration building screams and moans. Can you tell us from which part of the administration building you heard this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, the screams could be heard when the guard would come with a list if his hands and call out persons from various rooms. And then when these persons would be taken to the metal door, practically as soon as the metal door would close, practically the screams would follow immediately as soon as the metal door would close.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As soon as the metal door would close?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can I understand it this way, then, that the beatings took place immediately in the hallway, right after the metal door?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that people would start screaming just like that without any reason, which is not to say that they were not taken any further; however, the screaming would start immediately after the metal door in the case of certain persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you hear screams from other parts of the administration building, and where from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me, please, did your wife try to leave Foca unsuccessfully for a while?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did she finally manage to leave Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not give you the exact date when my wife left. My daughter left a bit earlier with the neighbours, and my wife thought that this infamous KP Dom done would be resolved before it had actually been resolved. She tried to wait for me and my son. However, when all hope was lost, then it was August or September, October, approximately, I can't tell you exactly what the date of her departure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that she was waiting for the situation to get better, but let us be quite precise. Just before she left Foca, did she try to leave but did not succeed in doing so?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already gave you an answer, that she did try.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know what Mr. Krnojelac's working hours were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say when Mr. Krnojelac came and left exactly, but it was regular working hours, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said, sir, that the border police slept in the restaurant across the street from the KP Dom. How far away is the border from Foca, from the KP Dom? Do you know that, the border with Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly how many kilometres away it is. It's about 30 to 40 kilometres. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you heard that Mr. Krnojelac, after his house had burned down, was staying at Dr. Sosevic's apartment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was that apartment owned by Dr. Sosevic or the KP Dom at that time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly whose property it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you own your apartment, or were you given that apartment by your company, and were you allowed to use it in that way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had what was called a tenant's right to this apartment that was owned by my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to explain to the Trial Chamber. This legal term that was used in Yugoslavia then when I say tenant's right. Who was the actual owner of the apartment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual owner was the [redacted]. However, after a while, a person does obtain the tenant's right to a particular apartment, and I had the tenant's right to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that to say that you had the right to use that apartment, but you did not have the right to sell the apartment, to put the money in your own pocket, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, people did not buy their apartments. That's why it was a privilege to have this tenant's right. Whoever would obtain a tenant's right would have the right to use this apartment in a way because in that way, a person would in part in a way become sort of owner of the apartment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You could exchange it, but could you sell it? Could you put the money in your own pocket?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, did Dr. Sosevic work in the KP Dom before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he worked there? Yes, he did. Whether he worked there all the time, I don't know, or whether he worked there only part time, I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know that after his house burnt down, Mr. Krnojelac spent a large part of 1992 in a hotel, the Zelengora Hotel where other refugees were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there were refugees at the hotel. As for Mr. Krnojelac, I did not know about him being at the hotel itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said today that once when a military truck took people out for an exchange, that another military truck was on the other side of the Drina. Can you tell us exactly where?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on the other side of the Drina. It was by the Drina River bank, but it was on the same side where the KP Dom is. At the parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how high the metal door is, the one that leads to the metalwork shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think it's a standard metal door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to explain to us what "standard" means?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean standard doors. I don't know, like a door, like, like, the door to this courtroom that we enter. Something like that. Of course, they were wider so that vehicles could also enter the compound of the metalwork shop itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We had a witness here who worked at the metalwork shop who said that he could see across that door when he would climb up onto a kiosk. How could you see the area in front of the KP Dom from the metalwork shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's simple to explain that. The workshop itself, the locksmith's workshop, the metalwork shop, the blacksmith's shop, the welder's shop, all of that was at the entrance into the metalwork shop as such. However, the mechanic's workshop is a bit further up, a bit higher in relation to the metal door, so I was a bit higher up than those who were down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say a bit higher up. Since you are a mechanic, can you tell us how high up this is, and how much higher were you in relation to the other part of the shop?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to tell, but -- it is hard to tell, but probably the difference in altitude could have been, say, a metre and a half or even two metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We took over your transcript from a different case that was related to the same area, so I'm just going to put a few questions to you in relation to that testimony. You talked about a period that you also referred to here in your examination-in-chief just before the war broke out, the 5th of April, the rally, et cetera. Did your son do his military service in the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My son did his military service in the army, and he was precisely in the conflict with the Croats, and the Croat Serbs and the army. He was at Petrova Gora. He was doing his military service there, and his term was extended for a month, a month and a half, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you take him out of the Yugoslav People's Army earlier than that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I get him out of the Yugoslav People's Army when his term was extended?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When did he leave the army?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said to us, sir, that you stood guard in Jelec a few times. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Which weapons did you have when you stood guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I had my father's rifle. This was a hunting rifle, a personal weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say a hunting rifle. Can you give us a closer description? Which ammunition was needed for this hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a hunting rifle, a two-barreled rifle, a 14-millimetre rifle, a number 14 as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did ethnic Serbs also take part in the guards in Jelec?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Jelec is practically 98 or 99 per cent Muslim in terms of its population, there are a few houses above Govza and a few above Poljica. They did not take part in these guards, at least, we were not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Major Besevic, and who is that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left Jelec, I'm not sure, it was the 29th or the 30th of April. I think it would be the 30th rather than the 29th. Except for the civilian population, the Muslim population which organised itself at its own initiative with a few hunting rifles, a few automatic rifles, a few M-48 rifles, there weren't any other weapons. And then this Besevic was not in Jelec. After that, rumour had it that after I had left he had stopped by in Jelec, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since you told us here about the rumours you heard concerning other stories, you say that he stopped by. What does that mean, that he stopped in passing or that he came with soldiers to organise the defence? Tell us, exactly what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like he was in passing, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: There was a witness here who was from Jelec who said that he had come with a certain number of soldiers, and that the people of Jelec wanted to hand over their weapons; however, that he organised fighting.

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I learned after I left. What kind of agreement was reached between Besevic and the population of Jelec, I really cannot talk about these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you returned to Foca on the 30th, around the 30th of April, until the 25th of May, was there a curfew that was on in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was this a curfew for all citizens?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard with my very own ears when a police vehicle with a loud speaker went all around town, and when they were saying that Muslims were prohibited from assembling in the street and moving about town, and that they were supposed to stay in their own homes. I heard that with my very own ears.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there a curfew for all citizens in Foca in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that because I did not leave my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that you came from Jelec because your wife was ill. Did you take her to see a doctor?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She had tonsillitis. She had a sore throat, and I had to take my wife somewhere. The war in Sarajevo had already started. I had to take my wife somewhere, Kalinovik, Miljevina, or Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you, sir. I'm sorry. We don't want to use up too much time. I'm just interested in what happened when you came back to Foca. Please just don't talk at the same time when I talk. Let's not speak at the same time. So when you came in Foca, did you take her to the doctor after that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How did she get better, then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lady who is my next door neighbour, she lived at the apartment to the right of my apartment. She brought some antibiotics and it is due to these antibiotics that my wife got well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is your next door neighbour a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What is she by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether she's a Hungarian or a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What about her husband, what ethnicity is he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said to us -- you talked to us in detail about how you were taken to the KP Dom and who took you. You mentioned that you knew three out of the four persons involved. Is it correct that when you arrived in the KP Dom, one of the persons who brought you in said to the guard to take you to Room 16?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So the person who arrested you, or, rather, who took you from your apartment to the KP Dom said to the guard to which room to take you exactly?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And were you taken to the room that this person said you should be taken to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This person who said to the guard which room you should be taken to, what did this person wear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Military camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-249 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
