utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Kuo. Is this your witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Stand up, please, sir. Would you please make the solemn declaration in the terms of the document which is being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. The pseudonym document will be Exhibit P441, and it is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, before you is a sheet of paper which is document P441, and on top of it you will see FWS-172. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Underneath that, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Beneath your name, is that your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Beneath your birth date, is that the profession that you had in Foca in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And below that, is that the name of the place where you were working in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, in 1992, how long had you been working at your profession?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I did my regular work in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Without telling us what you were doing because you've asked for us to keep this under seal, could you tell us how many years you were working at that profession?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I have a total of 38 years of service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In 1992, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you married?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm a widower.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When the war began in Foca in April 1992, were you at home?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you go to work during that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: When the war started in April, there was the first casualty, a neighbour of mine who was a policeman. I asked for two days' sick leave to attend the funeral of this man who was killed. That man was a policeman. [redacted], and he was the first casualty in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: After the sick leave to attend his funeral, did you go back to work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes. I came back to work, and on my way to work from home, we made a detour. I had boarded a bus going downtown, and when we reached the army hall, we saw that all the windows had been broken and there were automatic weapons pointed at the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How long did you stay at work?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: At that time I stayed at work. I was sort of repaying other colleagues working their shifts so that from the 11th of April until the 25th of April, I didn't leave the hospital at all because it was impossible to leave the hospital compound. The bus didn't run any longer, and it was dangerous to take that road because the plateau in front of the hospital was under constant attack from the surrounding hills. It was covered with bursts of gunfire, so it was unsafe to leave or to come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, you said, sir, that you were at the hospital until the 25th of April. Was the hospital functioning at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The hospital was functioning around the clock. It was receiving wounded and sick people who were coming in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did it receive patients of one ethnicity or another?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The hospital admitted all patients who came in asking for help.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you notice whether the patients were civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Most of them were civilians. One evening we admitted four people wounded by shells from Foca itself. It was around 1.00 we received several patients from Visegrad, including some elderly people and several women.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity those four from Visegrad were?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: All of them were Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was the hospital ever taken over by Serb military?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: After four or five days, I'm not sure of the date, it might have been the 15th or the 16th, the army took over the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: In what way did they take it over?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: One evening they simply walked in. Nobody offered any resistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did the military change the way the hospital was being run?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The hospital worked normally. The soldiers introduced themselves as the Serbian guard, White Eagles, Arkan's men, and locals who were hiding their faces. At least, some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were the Serb forces armed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: All of them were armed with automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did any of them ever interfere with the admission of patients into the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: In the first two or three days, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Later, on the 16th or the 17th, they personally brought two wounded Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know where they were brought from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They were brought from a place near Foca. One came from a village called Sukovac, and the other one was from downtown. I know the names of these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names, please. Uzeir Cankusic was wounded in his shoulder, in his right shoulder

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And the second person?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: And the second person was an auto mechanic, Ibro Selimovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened when Mr. Cankusic and Mr. Selimovic were brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: That was in the evening hours, and the medical team on duty, Dr. Supic, a surgeon, and Dr. Aziz Torlak, also a surgeon, wanted to admit these two and keep them for treatment because they were in need of medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were they allowed to stay?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The people who brought them didn't allow it, so the men were just bandaged and taken back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know -- you mentioned that Mr. Cankusic was injured in the shoulder. Do you know specifically what injuries he had?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: His injuries were inflicted by firearms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And Mr. Selimovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He was beaten up, and his ribs were fractured.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, you said the guards who brought Mr. Cankusic and Mr. Selimovic to the hospital would not let them stay and receive treatment. Do you know why they were brought there at all?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I don't know why. They took them back immediately, but they brought them again the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened the next morning when they were brought back?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The next morning the surgical team on duty wanted to admit them once again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who brought them the next morning?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They were brought by two uniformed military men. One of them was referred to as Vojvoda, which means the duke. I didn't know who the man was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were they members of the Serb military?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They were members of what was called the Serbian guard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And were those two men allowed to be treated by the surgical team?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: As I said, the surgeons were not allowed to give them medical assistance. Instead, they were taken through -- across the compound of the hospital and outside the compound, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was it just those two men, or was there anybody else with them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Since I was at my workplace, I could see only two of them in the hallway which was next to me. They were taken outside the compound, and perhaps five or 600 metres away from the hospital they were found dead the next day. They had been killed. And another person, another wounded man who had spent the night at the hospital had been taken away with them. His name was Adnan Isanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Isanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He had been taken away with them and killed, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How do you know that they were killed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Some passersby came in to the hospital and told us that it had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know who killed them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I didn't see it, but I know who took them away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who took them away? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The people I mentioned, the one called Vojvoda and his escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did either of those two men make any comments before these three men were led away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The one who called himself Vojvoda told the surgeon that they were finished, that he personally would cure them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you ever see the bodies of those three men who were killed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The corpses were collected and brought to the hospital morgue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Is that where you saw them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I saw them and several other people who were identified by Dr. Zijo Ajanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Cankusic and Mr. Selimovic were taken, where they spent the night before this happened, from the first visit to the hospital to the second?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They told me that they had spent the night at the KP Dom, the former prison, and that they couldn't get any sleep from the pain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: That sick man, the men told me that when they came again the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were there ever any incidents where soldiers at the hospital shot at anyone?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Soldiers didn't shoot at the staff at the hospital. On one occasion there was a van going along the left bank of the Drina River carrying five, six, or ten women and children, and from the compound they shot at them with automatic weapons, and they hit the driver. The van swerved and crashed into the cemetery called Patkovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were any of the injured from that crash brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes. The driver was shot dead in the head, and some women and children were brought to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that vehicle a military vehicle or civilian, do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: It was a civilian van, and inside, inside the van were only women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What ethnicity were the women and children and driver?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They were of Muslim or Bosniak ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What direction were they headed when they were shot?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They were going towards Gorazde along the left bank of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were any staff members from the hospital taken away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: After that, some staff were taken away. On the 24th of April, Dr. Aziz Torlak was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you also taken away at some point?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I was taken away together with two of my colleagues on the 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you were taken away? Were you taken from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: That afternoon, around five, half past five, I don't remember exactly, I was called to come to the gate of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why were you called there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Allegedly to give a statement of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who was at the gate of the hospital when you got there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: There were soldiers, guards, and one security man from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you about what you should do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Since I was wearing my work clothes, they told me to go back and get dressed, to change.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did they tell you why?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They didn't say anything as to why, but I went back, changed, and they told me that I'm going to -- that I was going to give a statement, and then I would be taken back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: We were taken directly outside the KP Dom. There were no statements at all, nothing. They turned us over directly to the guard of the KP Dom, which was a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were not taken alone. Who else was taken with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They took Enver Cemo, and Izet Causevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Are you able to identify who took you there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I'm not sure about their names, but there was -- one of them was Banovic, nicknamed Bota, and one town policeman by the name of Mate. I don't know his last name. We called him Mate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The person you identified --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: And there was one other man whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: The person you identified by the nickname Bota, what was his --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What was his position, or what kind of uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Both of them wore military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Cemo and Mr. Causevic are of what ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Bosniaks, the same as I.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know whether any Serb hospital personnel were allowed to continue working?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes. They went to work regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that even after your arrest?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They worked even after my arrest, and even some Bosniak staff continued to work after my arrest. I don't know for how long because I was away. I had already been taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And to return just very briefly to the person named Bota, did you ever hear what happened to him later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I was going to say something more about what happened to the wounded people who arrived at the hospital from the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you want to say about them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I wanted to say that those wounded people from Foca were taken care of. They were very seriously wounded. Some of them underwent surgery, and two persons, when the hospital had already been taken over, were taken away to Sarajevo by the Medicins Sans Frontieres for maxial facial surgery. And Nikola Koljevic accompanied those Medicins Sans Frontieres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What time period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: That was the period when wounded people were coming in from Foca and Visegrad, the period before the takeover of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Regarding Bota, could you tell us if you heard what happened to him later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I heard when we were in that camp, we were being classified into work groups according to our skills. There was a construction work group, there was a group of craftsmen, mechanics, and drivers. The mechanics, locksmiths, and electricians were engaged in the dissembling of construction machinery in the town, and those machines were brought to a place above our quarters beneath an awning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps you didn't understand my question. You identified one of the men who took you to KP Dom by the name Banovic with the nickname Bota. Did you ever hear what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: In relation to these men, those who went out to work in the construction group, we found out that Bota -- or, rather, that Milorad Krnojelac's sons, the warden's sons, were wounded somewhere around Tjentiste, that they ran into a minefield.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And was Bota also involved in the vehicle that ran over the minefield?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Allegedly, yes. Bota and one or two of the warden's sons. I don't know for sure, but that is the piece of news that went through the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the KP Dom, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: When I arrived in the KP Dom, they put me in a transit room, and those two who came with me, too, Cemo and Causevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What room was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Room 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How long were you kept in Room 12?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Until I got out. Until the 30th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: During your time at KP Dom, were you ever interrogated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I can't remember the date of interrogation because first I was interrogated by Koprivica nicknamed Kopi, I can't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you make a statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I gave part of the statement, and then a huge man walked in. He was in military uniform, or rather, his trousers belonged to a military uniform, and he also had a shirt with short sleeves, and then they talked, and then the whole thing was interrupted and he told me that it would be continued the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was it continued?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: However, it was not continued. Perhaps 15 days went by.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What happened after 15 days?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: After 15 days, I was called in for an interrogation, and I was interrogated by Zoran Vladicic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I did sign this statement about him interrogating me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you sign a statement during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Well, during the interrogation. He was interrogating me, and there was this statement, and he offered it to me, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were you threatened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I tried to read the statement. He didn't let me. He said to me, "Do you want me to write that, `I killed ten persons?'"

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: He wanted -- he threatened that he would write down that you killed ten persons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What did you do when he said that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I said you can do whatever you want, but my conscience is clear. I said, you can check with my colleagues. From the 10th till the 20th, or rather, 25th of April, I never left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you sign the statement then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I did sign the statement, and he accused me of being commander of a medical corps squad. I said to him that I'm not even a military conscript, as I was not. It is true that I was a commander of a military squad at the time when I did my military service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How many years ago was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: You mean when I did my military service? I did my military service in 1950.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Sir, while you were detained at the KP Dom, were you ever beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: They did not beat me physically, but there was terrible torture during the interrogation. It would have been easier for me to have been beaten than to have been insulted that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you mean by the torture during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Provocative questions. They were saying things that were impossible, that I had weapons, that I was an organiser of the resistance. Since I was an old man, I did not -- I could not have been involved in anything like that, nor were there any grounds for that. And I was at my working place all the time when all of that was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did that make you feel, the way you were treated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Well, I felt that the worst would happen, that there would be beatings. At one moment, I almost felt sick.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know if other detainees were beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Other detainees will say. I did not see that, so I cannot maintain that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the sound of people being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When would you hear the sounds?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Not during the day, but during the night when they took them out after this tragedy that occurred with Krnojelac's son and Bota, we were all terribly afraid. Sometime in mid-June, people were taken out during the night, five or four persons at a time. Screams could be heard, yelling, and footsteps in the part of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Are you able to identify people who were taken out and beaten in this way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I can identify quite a few such persons because seven were taken out of the room that I was in. I can mention the names and surnames of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Kuloglija Mustafa was taken out among the first. Husein Rikalo. His brother, Necko Rikalo, Meho Pasovic, Nurko Niksic, Salem Bico, Amer Frasto.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll just go back --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: And from other rooms, other people were taken. In the morning when we would go to breakfast, in front of Room 12, some of the people I knew did not show up. Among others, there was Zulfo Veiz, a policeman; Dzano Vahida, a policeman; Munib Veiz, a sales person; Adnan Granov, Abdurahman Cankusic, Refik Cankusic, nicknamed Pepi. These were two brothers, the two Soro brothers, Suljo and Seval, and Alija Altoka, Nail Hodzic, Ramo Dzendusic, and I could not mention everyone now. While all of this was fresh in my memory, I wrote all of them down, so perhaps I would need that to refresh my memory. My memory is the way it is after nine years, after all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When did you prepare the list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Just after I got out of prison while my memory was still fresh.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Why did you make a list of these people?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Well, since I got out of prison, I thought that members of their families would ask them -- ask me where they were and what happened to them. I did not think that this would happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You didn't think what would happen?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Trial, testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: On what basis did you compile your list? Did you say it was just from your memory because your memory was still fresh?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The basis of my memory, and also there were a few of us who got out of prison, and then we talked. It was a longish list, some 35, 36 men, because 35 of us were set free.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What year was that when you compiled the list?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The month of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to have the witness shown this list which is marked ID 299. The English version is ID 299/A.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, I will not ask you specific questions about what's on the list, but just ask you to identify that in fact you prepared that list.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I stand by this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And you said one of the reasons you prepared the list was in case family members of those people asked you about them. Did, in fact, family members approach you and ask about the people who are on your list?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes. I have close relatives on this list, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were the family members -- let me ask it to you this way: Do you know if any of these people were ever seen again after they disappeared from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Not a single one of them has ever been seen since. In addition to this, I will mention some bigger groups. I can even remember some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: We'll get to that if a few moments.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution wishes to enter into evidence exhibit -- ID 299 and 299/A as Prosecution Exhibit P299 and 299/A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there any objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be Exhibits P299 and P299/A. Do they need to be under seal? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, and also for the Court's convenience, we've prepared what we have marked as -- it's not in the trial binders, but it should be ID 299/A/1 which is an annotated copies, annotated version of the list. So it will have on it the schedule references where these names appear. We've given a copy to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would be very helpful. Is there any objection to it, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know until we get a copy. As far as I understood it, we haven't got a copy of that that is being mentioned just now. What my learned friend is referring to now is, is it ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: It's actually the -- it's the English version of 299, and it has been annotated with just handwritten numbers next to the names, for instance, C-19 or B whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Except that we haven't got 299/A. We have A/1, but we haven't got 299/A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I suspect that 299/A/1 is a copy of 299/A with the handwriting on it. That's the way Ms. Kuo has described it. Is that right, Ms. Kuo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, then we have no objections to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P299/A/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, the list that you -- that we've referred to that is now 299, you've given it the title "The list of people taken away in groups from Foca KP Dom in the period between 26 June, 1992, and 15 July 1992." Of the people on the list, do you know whether any of them were beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: It is these people. They were beaten in that interval. I remember that well. Literally, we were coming back from dinner. I'm going to tell you about a particular case, chronologically. Niksic, Nurko and Konjo Halim were coming back from dinner, and the guard Obrenovic said that they should report to the administration, and they reported. We went to the room. Since both of them were from my room, I became restless. I was really concerned. Late in the evening, between 9.00 and 10.00, I went up to the window because from Room 12, I could not see the exit through the administrative building. I just heard a scream. I just heard screams and yelling. They were shouting at the top of their lungs. Somebody called out, "Nurko" in a really loud voice twice, "Nurko, Nurko." And then there was no sound after that. Perhaps about half an hour, an hour later a shot, a pistol shot rang out, tuk-tuk-tuk-tuk. That meant that it wasn't only the two of them. That's how it ended, that particular evening. They never appeared again in the compound in any room, let alone our room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How many shots did you hear?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: After those five shots, did you hear anything else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: A car was heard several times, several evenings. It had a problem with the exhaust pipe. It had a special sound. Whenever it came to the prison, to the camp, people would disappear. I cannot tell you chronologically now who these people were because there was such great fear and anxiety as to who would be next. Usually the guard would come to the door and call out some names, and then they would take them to the administration building, and then we could no longer see them. I couldn't see. I can't talk about others, what they could see and what they could not see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you tell what direction the car with the broken exhaust pipe was going after those five shots that night?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Towards town. We couldn't see, but towards town; or towards the bridge, or towards town. Because the exit facing the bridge was 40 or 50 metres lower, and the other one was bigger, the one facing town, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was it still daylight or was it already nighttime when the car came and left?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Nighttime, nighttime invariably. Never during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you remember what date that was when Nurko Niksic and Halim Konjo disappeared?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but it was sometime around mid-June. Not only them, all of those who are listed here, over 35 names, that is, in various intervals. Sometimes it would be one or two days, and then a break, and then again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You said the guard Obrenovic called out Nurko Niksic and Halim Konjo. Do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Obren was his nickname, and to tell you the truth, I wouldn't know his real name. A big man, really big.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a guard by the name of Dragomir Obrenovic on Exhibit P3 at number 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Before that last time when you saw Nurko Niksic, did you see him come back from being beaten, with injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes. Once before he was taken out for an interrogation. He was returned to the same room. Dr. Torlak was among us, and also Dr. Ibro Karovic. We wrapped him in wet sheets. For two or three days he couldn't go out for breakfast and lunch. We had to bring his meals to the room. Then he got better, and then in about ten or 15 days, what I talked about previously happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Could you describe the injuries that Nurko Niksic had when you saw him return to your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He was black and blue all over his body, on his chest, legs, arms, and his face.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Haematoma.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if Dr. Aziz Torlak himself was ever beaten at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Aziz Torlak? On one occasion since we had worked together, he complained to me. Somebody asked him for the key to his car. His car was at the hospital. They took his car away, and he was -- he had been cut a bit up here. He just showed this to me, and then he hid it again very fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I had my head down when he indicated that. Where did he indicate?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, when you said he had a cut here, you indicated the neck area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: A bit of his neck, over here, a bit of his neck, a small cut, very small cut. He came to give his car keys. He had a new Golf.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who did Dr. Torlak say cut him on the neck?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He didn't want to tell me. He said if we managed to survive, people will know. He was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether it was a prison staff, like a guard, or was it a soldier, or somebody from the outside?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Not somebody from the prison staff, somebody from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But was this during the time when he was detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He was detained at the KP Dom, yes. And we were together in this transit Room 12.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: My question was specifically about when he received the injury. Did he receive the injury while he was at KP Dom, or before he was brought there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: While he was at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see injuries on any other detainees?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I did. I did see injuries. On Enes Uzunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What injuries did --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Izet Causevic, Hajro Sabanovic, Avdo Mehmedspahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: And, and Salko Mandzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What injuries did you see on Mr. Uzunovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Enes Uzunovic, he had bruises all over his body.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did he tell you how he got them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He didn't say. He didn't dare talk about it. He just waved his hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: But did he sustain the injuries while he was at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Enes Uzunovic is listed in the indictment at paragraph 5.29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: As well as on Schedule C, number 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And Witness, what kind of injuries did you see on Izet Causevic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: There were bruises on his face.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How did he sustain those?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: At the interrogation, when he was interrogated he sustained those injuries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that also at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What injuries did you see on Hajro Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Bruises all over his body. He sustained those on his -- upon his arrival at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He was lying in my room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did he tell you who beat him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Burilo -- what's his name? I don't remember. He was nicknamed Busi.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Was that a guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes. He was a guard at the KP Dom, a full-time employee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the incident with Hajro Sabanovic is in the indictment, paragraph 5.23, and there is a guard named Burilo -- we're looking for the specific reference to the guard Burilo, but I think he's been mentioned several times before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He certainly has. But we've got the exhibit number, too, haven't we, anyway, on the record here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: He's number 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 56, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, what injuries did you see on Avdo Mehmedspahic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Avdo Mehmedspahic worked at the pharmacy, and for a long time he hid in his apartment. And when he asked to get out, to be released at the end of June, instead of that he was brought to the prison, and he was beaten up. He told me that he never knew who was beating him. He just lost a tooth, and he couldn't even eat a slice of bread. And for two or three days, he was unable to go to eat. He lay in his room until he recovered. He was also in my room. And he said at the end when he came to, that this same Burilo gave him a glass of brandy to come round, and said that nobody would touch him again. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mehmedspahic say that Burilo beat him as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about who beat him. Maybe he didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Avdo Mehmedspahic is listed in Schedule B at number 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And finally, Salko Mandzo, what injuries did you see him with?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: On Salko Mandzo when he was being taken away, I saw a cut next to his eye, a cut made with a sharp object. And when he was brought back to our room, they didn't let him stay there. A guard stood by waiting for him until he collected his things, and he was immediately taken to another room lest he told us who had done it and what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Witness, you said when -- that you saw this cut on Mr. Mandzo when he was being taken away. Do you know how he received that cut? Had he been taken out already, received the cut, and then came back?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He came back with that cut. He didn't tell us how he sustained it because he had no time. The guard stood by in the room while he collected his things, and he was taken to another room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, Salko Mandzo is listed in the indictment at paragraph 5.28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were detainees kept in solitary confinement; do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know why they would be put there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: When people were brought to the prison, the prison authorities logged them up according to some categorisation of their own and according to people's conduct in the prison itself. If somebody, for instance, queued twice for lunch to take two meals, they would be put into solitary confinement, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you ever hear people being beaten in the solitary confinement cells?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: In the part where I was, I wasn't close to solitary cells and I couldn't hear it, whereas in other parts of the quarters, other inmates said they could hear and that there were beatings. And one more thing, if I may say, there were not enough solitary cells, so the prisoners themselves built additional solitary cells to increase their number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say the prisoners themselves built it, was it on the order of the KP Dom administration?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: On the order of the KP Dom administration, and house painting works were done by Fehim Dedovic and other works were done by Salcinovic, Nusret.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: You mentioned at the beginning of your testimony that there were several work groups formed. When you ever a part of those work groups?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: No. Only once did I go to unload something. That happened only once, because I was an elderly man and they always chose younger people, stronger people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Where did you unload things?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I unloaded some foodstuffs at Mose Pijade street at a building called Brena together with another inmate by the name of Zuko Sefkija.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who took you to unload the foodstuffs?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: We were taken out by a guard, and there we found one uniformed man, and in the vehicle there was the same town policeman by the name of Mate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you say a uniformed man, what kind of uniform was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: It was a military camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Do you know for whom that foodstuff was meant?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: We unloaded that food into a shop. We didn't load anything, we just unloaded the food. I don't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you have a choice about whether to go do this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: No. A guard came and called our names out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Approximately when was this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: That was sometime in June. I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned that when people were taken out of the rooms, many of them disappeared. When they were taken out, were they told where they were being taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: The people who were taken out during the night, somebody would come to the door and call out their names. They were taken to the administration building and screams and yelling were heard, and those people were never seen again. Those are the people from this list that I mentioned. In other groups -- or perhaps you wanted to ask something Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No. Go on, you said, "In other groups."

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: On one occasion, sometime in June, a large group of prisoners was put together and taken out. They told us when they came back about where they had been. There had been women and children. They were taken to the road towards Pljevlja near Cajnice. There was some kind of British mission there, and some sort of fake exchange for Serbian soldiers had been organised. However, this group of people just spent the night and came back. The exchange didn't take place. They didn't know the reason why, and none of us knew it, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Were there other people taken out for exchange who actually did not return?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: As for other people, I remember another group. On the 25th of August, that group was taken out sometime in the afternoon, and there were 18 people, as far as I could count. And on the 27th of August, another 20 men were taken out, as far as I could see - I could only see their heads over the wall - and before they left, they were lined up in the hallway. I can remember some names. I don't remember how many of them there were, 34, 5, or 6. Among them were Saban Durak, Hajro Sabanovic, Enver Sabanovic, Zaim Rikalo. A man called Culup [phoen], I don't remember his name. Mumin Kameric, Dejro Cankusic, and Esad Soro, a brother of Hadzi Mesic. I remember those people from those two groups. Those people left carrying their things, and they had told us they were going for an exchange. It's been nine years now, and I have never heard of any of them, and I never heard that any of them had reappeared. The next group was a large one, and I was in that group. We were informed that people over 60 and people with some sort of a health problem and underage persons were in it. They made a list of 55 persons. It was on the 29th of August. They took us out to the dining room, a large room, and we spent there several hours until dark. Then there was some sort of commotion and transfer from that part of the building which was nearer to the hospital. Rooms 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15, all of these rooms were transferred to the other side. And the group of people, whom I didn't manage to count because it was dark already, was taken to the gate towards the administration building. I don't remember how many there were. I remember only one man who had been in solitary confinement. His name was Sahmanovic, and his nickname name was Ace. He was running across the compound wearing a wind breaker, and he waved to us standing in the dining room: "Here I go, I'm leaving before you." We kept waiting in that room. We didn't leave that night. Instead, we were taken back to the transit Room 12, all 55 of us, and we spent the entire night there. Some people got their 40 winks, and then in the other -- the next morning, a bus came. We all filed out to the courtyard. We boarded the bus, and we set off. We didn't know where. We received no papers, nothing. We didn't know whether we were being released or not. In front of the administration building there was Savo Todovic. He was standing there. Some people from downtown had come, Pasovic's father-in-law, for instance, came to say good-bye. At the bus station we stopped, and citizens were standing there waiting, including citizens of Serb ethnicity. Some had brought some food, bread. Some people even brought a bottle of spirits. Nobody entered the buses. Then we went on towards Brod, Scepan Polje, making stops.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, let me just interrupt you there. When you -- when all 55 of you were put on the bus, were you exchanged immediately, or were you brought back to KP Dom later that same day, on the 30th of August?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: We were not exchanged. There was no exchange. We travelled to Niksic, and Pero Elez and Dragan Gagovic intercepted us just outside Niksic, some ten kilometres before Niksic, and they sent us back. We didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Let me stop you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Who was Dragan Gagovic? Do you know what his official position was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: He was the commander of the police station in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: When you were returned to the KP Dom that day --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they took us back there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: -- were some of the group of 55 separated from each other?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: When they took us back, we waited for a long time at Scepan Polje. We didn't know what was going on. We were all afraid. When we arrived at the KP Dom, everyone was surprised, including the guards. What is this? They took us somewhere, to some room where we had something to eat, and they took us all to Room 11. There were not enough beds because of that transfer which preceded our departure, so we put beds together two by two and we asked for some blankets. However, nothing came of it. We stayed for only about half an hour. I stood by the door and I was wondering whether they were going to give us those blankets. Then a guard came and called out ten names. Those people picked up their things and left. Then another half an hour later, another ten names were called out, and the guard told these people to pick up their things and follow him. Where these people left, we have no clue. I never heard that any one of them was ever heard of again. And I can give you some names, the names I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: What distinguished those 20 people from the 35 that were not called out in that way?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what was the reason. There was only one elderly man among them. The rest of them were younger people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: And of the 35 who were not called out, were those younger or older men?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Well, most of them were elderly, frail people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: If you remember the names --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Including myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: If you've remembered the names of those 20 who were called out and you never heard from them again, could you please give them to us?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me, I have it written on a piece of paper. There are about 13 names. I cannot tell you who they are by heart. There was Izet Causevic; he was an arts teacher. Asim Mujic, a lawyer. He usually distributed food at the kitchen. Murat Granov, Mezbur Rasim and his brother. Maja Blacevic, Nedzib Lojo, Ismet Pasovic and his cousin nicknamed Pace, Ibro Ovcina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I cannot remember all the names. It's been a long time. I have it all written down. None of those people were ever seen or heard of again, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, the piece of paper that you mentioned where you wrote these names down, when did you write the names down?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: When I left. In fact, when the 35 of us were taken out again, we took the same road again, but first they took us back to Velecevo where some sort of command was based. They took us there for some sort of checkup, and then they took us along the same road to Montenegro, and then we reached Podgorica which was earlier called Titograd, around 1.00 or 2.00. Around 5.00, we reached Rozaje. There were no papers given to us. A guard just said, "You are free to go. There are other refugees here. Do what you want." And the group of about 20 of us went to Murhamet, the Muslim charity organisation, and the Red Cross. They couldn't admit us, but they transferred us by bus to some sort of collection centre in Krajcinovic Banja, and that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us, when did you write down the names on that piece of paper? That was the question. How long after this release did you write down those names on the piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: I wrote that down when I returned to Bosnia in 1995, and I had already forgotten some names during -- by the time that I gave my statements to investigators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you write them down in 1995 at about the same time that you spoke to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: FWS-172
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, Ms. Kuo, I think we might come back to that in the morning. I want to raise an issue about this motion that we've received. Is this your matter or is it Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff's?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I can handle it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I just wanted to know whose it was, first of all. Have you spoken to the Defence about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think I will handle it. I will handle it. We have spoken about it, and it is not a problem. They received this morning, they received the documents that we have on this witness, and we do not have much. It's just the Bosnian statement and one little memo about the telephone conversation. And as far as I understood, Mr. Bakrac, they agree to have this person testify and have enough time to prepare for the date that is proposed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is during the week of the 2nd of April. Is that so, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. However, the Defence suggested that we could hear the witness even this week if the Office of the Prosecutor managed to bring him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we'll see what the Prosecution can do. Have you got any objection to the -- other than the usual objection, to the protective measures sought?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The usual objection of this Defence stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then those protective measures will be granted, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. I don't think we need to enter a formal order because we've done it orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now if you can bring the witness along, whenever you can get the witness along.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually I was mistaken when I discussed the matter with Mr. Bakrac. I thought this witness was actually coming tomorrow, tomorrow evening, and he could be on the stand on Thursday. But this witness is actually coming only on Wednesday evening, and of course, we have to talk with him first because we do not want to hear his entire story, but some very focussed matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'd be very grateful?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And that's why we would like to have a discussion with him first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We would be very grateful if you could focus every witness's evidence. Very well, we'll adjourn now until 9.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
